verdict.rationale:
ROADMAP GATE — RATIONALE FOR: keep

Recommendation (derived in code, not by this writer): **keep**. Rule that fired: "no kill criterion hit, backlog value (400.15) covers projected cost, 2/3 metrics met → keep." What follows explains that determination against the inputs it was computed from; it does not re-weigh or second-guess the recommendation.

1. Kill criteria
No kill criterion fired (kill_criteria hit: none), and none were left undetermined (kill_criteria that could not be determined: none) — every kill criterion in scope was evaluated cleanly against available data and none tripped. On this leg the rule's premise is fully supported.

2. Metrics vs targets (2/3 met)
- Healthy launches promoted to prod through /launch + /deploy: target ≥1, actual 1 — MET.
- Human actions from Brief to live URL: target 2, actual 2 (sign brief, approve launch) — MET.
- Seeded-regression drills that auto-roll back without a human: target ≥1, actual reported as NOT MET (seeded_regression_reached_prod = 0; the one observed rollback-without-a-human is not confirmed as a seeded-regression case).

Flag: this third metric is inconsistent across the two input sections. It is scored "met: false" in metrics_vs_targets, but it is *also* listed under "metrics that could not be measured" with the reason "telemetry does not cover it." Per the stated convention, an unmeasured metric is neither met nor missed — so recording it simultaneously as a hard "false" and as "unmeasurable" is a contradiction in the inputs themselves. The practical effect on the recommendation is limited (the rule only needs 2 of 3 met, and it already has 2 unambiguous MET results from the other two metrics), but the "2/3 met" framing implies a clean measurement that this metric didn't actually get. Flagging this plainly rather than resolving it — the recommendation is unchanged.

3. Backlog value vs. "projected cost"
Remaining backlog value is given as 400.15 (sum of expected_value × confidence across all 8 ranked opportunities). The rule's stated justification is that this figure "covers projected cost." No "projected cost" number appears anywhere in the provided inputs — only historical burn (tokens 13,817,293; $41.15; 6 human-minutes) and the original ProjectBrief budget (3,000,000 tokens; $10; 0.5 human-hours) are given. Nothing here forecasts future cost. Readers should treat "covers projected cost" as a term the rule asserts but that these inputs cannot substantiate — it may be computed elsewhere in the pipeline, but it isn't visible here for verification.

4. Burn and budget status
budget_exhausted is reported as true, and the numbers bear that out on two of three axes: dollars burned ($41.15) are ~4.1x the $10 ProjectBrief budget, and tokens burned (13.8M) are ~4.6x the 3M budget. Human time is the exception — 6 minutes burned against a 30-minute (0.5 hour) budget, well under. So "budget_exhausted" is true on cost, not on human attention. This matters as context for a "keep" call: the venture has already run well past its planned dollar and token budget, and the "keep" recommendation is being made *after* that overrun, not before it.

5. Ranked opportunities
All 8 identified opportunities are marked within_budget: false, top-ranked by score being the canary-probe gap (opp-p5-2, 0.119), the ledger false-zero (opp-p5-5, 0.095), and the promoted-artifact/trunk reconciliation gap (opp-p5-1, 0.085). None of them can be funded from what remains of the current budget — consistent with budget_exhausted being true. The top-ranked item (opp-p5-2) is the one directly tied to the unmet/unmeasured metric discussed in §2: the canary watch's five hard-coded probe shapes don't exercise the `?q` query-parameter path that caused the real regression, so a repeat of that exact failure class would still read as healthy and would not auto-roll back.

Summary for the human deciding at this gate: the rule's three conditions are met as computed — no kill criterion hit, 2 of 3 metrics met, and a backlog-value figure the rule treats as sufficient — but two things in the underlying numbers deserve attention before acting on "keep": the third metric's double status (missed vs. unmeasurable) is self-contradictory, and "covers projected cost" rests on a quantity not present in these inputs. Cost burn is already ~4x over the ProjectBrief's dollar and token budget, even though human-time burn is low. None of this changes the recommendation being reported here, which remains keep.

draft_work_items.title: Drive the canary probe from a declared route set that covers every documented query parameter
draft_work_items.intent: The probe's request list is hard-coded in substrate/deploy.js and covers five shapes, none of which sends ?q or exercises DELETE. That is why three rounds of canary watch reported a zero error rate for a build whose ?q handler was broken, and why the defect that produced 263 prod 500s was caught by a human-facing sev1 path rather than by auto-rollback. Move the probe's route set out of the CLI and into the project's workspace configuration, seeded by /create-project from the documented API surface, so every query parameter the README describes (?q, ?sort, ?limit and their combinations) is exercised each round, and add an expected-status field per route so the probe can count a wrong 200 or an unexpected 4xx as an error instead of only counting 5xx and unreachable. Keep the verdict rule itself in the /deploy script where it lives today — this changes what is measured, not who decides. Done means: a seeded ?q regression on the canary produces a regressed verdict in round 1 and an automatic rollback, and the existing substrate/test/deploy.test.js cases still pass.

draft_work_items.title: Append a ledger entry straight from the run output file, with a wall clock that cannot be typed wrong
draft_work_items.intent: Recording a run today is three commands and a retyped JSON object: run-output.js prints agents and tokens_by_model, the operator pastes them into ledger append along with hand-typed started and finished timestamps, then reads the result back with ledger summary. The retyping has already corrupted the ledger — m2-maintain-triage carries wall_clock_sec 0 next to 338,559 tokens, and every summary reading it is wrong by that much. Add `ledger append --from-output <task.output>` that reads agents, tokens_by_model, the run result and both timestamps out of the output file itself, so --tokens-by-model and --started become overrides rather than required input, and make append refuse a wall_clock_sec of 0 on a run with non-zero tokens instead of writing it. Print the per-run cost and the by-model split on append so the operator needs no second command to see what the run cost. Keep every existing flag working, add a regression test for the impossible-zero refusal, and either backfill or explicitly mark the one bad row rather than leaving it to skew the Method Ledger. This moves none of the three stated success metrics; it protects the ledger those metrics are eventually read from.

draft_work_items.title: Reconcile promoted artifacts with main and fail preflight when prod's live sha is behind the trunk
draft_work_items.intent: A promotion currently ends at a running process: /deploy starts the canary sha on the prod port, writes a LaunchRecord and stops. Nothing merges the promoted artifact_ref into main, and nothing notices when a rollback leaves prod on an older sha than the trunk. The result is visible in the repo today: the ?offset feature this venture was briefed to build was promoted to prod from integration/c1v and is in no commit reachable from HEAD, and prod is presently running bfb99434, which predates the ?q fix main already carries. Add two things. First, a post-promotion step in /deploy that records the promoted sha's relationship to main and either fast-forwards main to the promoted artifact or emits an explicit unmerged-promotion item, so a promoted branch can never be garbage-collected with the only copy of shipped work on it. Second, a preflight check in /launch that reads prod's live sha from the deployment record, compares it to the trunk, and fails the go/no-go when prod is behind main on commits touching the app — the same check surfaces the current 'fix drafted but never relaunched' state instead of leaving a human to spot it in a HealthReport. Both are additive; no existing route or test changes.

draft_work_items.title: Count every gate on the Brief-to-URL path, escalations included, when reporting human actions
draft_work_items.intent: One of the three success metrics in the Brief is 'human actions from Brief to live URL', targeted at exactly two: sign the brief, approve the launch. The telemetry reports it as 1 + 1 = 2 while its own breakdown records a third action on the same path — an escalation gate between spec and implement that the design does not budget for — and the ledger cannot arbitrate because human_min is missing from 20 of its 28 rows. The metric therefore reads green on a path that cost three decisions. Make the count derive from the gate queue rather than a hand-kept table: have substrate/gates.js record, on every decision, the run_id and the stretch it belongs to; have ledger append derive human_min from the decided gates attached to that run instead of accepting it as an optional flag; and have the Improve usage stage count the metric as every decided gate whose run lies between the signed Brief and the promoted LaunchRecord, escalations and sev1 pages included, reported as designed-versus-actual. The target of 2 does not change; what changes is that a third action can no longer be invisible. Done means the c1 path reports 3 against a design of 2, and that gap is the number the Venture Verdict argues about.

draft_work_items.title: Tell the client when GET /items truncated the list, without breaking the bare-array response
draft_work_items.intent: This is wi-imp-1, already in the improve backlog as a synthetic drill item; the Phase 5 numbers turn it into a measured one, and it should be scheduled on that evidence rather than re-proposed as a second copy. GET /items applies the cap with a slice and returns a bare JSON array, so a client that asked for 25 and got 25 cannot tell a full page from a truncated one. The measured cost of that ambiguity is 388 capped responses in a three-hour window and 241 blind re-requests with a wider limit within five seconds. The Spec Writer should pick the carrier that does not break the existing contract — a response header reporting the unpaged match count (the result length after the ?q filter and before the cap) is the additive option, since every current test and client asserts on a bare array; an envelope is a breaking change and needs its own decision. Whatever the carrier, the count must be computed after filtering and before capping so it agrees with the filter -> sort -> cap pipeline, must be present on every GET /items response rather than only capped ones, and the README's ?limit section must document it. It moves none of the three line success metrics — it is client-facing product value, and the verdict at the Roadmap Gate should treat it that way.

draft_work_items.title: Cut the cost of the verify-fix loop, which is 72% of this venture's spend and 4x its budget
draft_work_items.intent: Measured over the whole ledger, this venture has spent $41.15 against a $10 Brief budget and 13.8M tokens against 3M, and build-implement accounts for 72% of the dollars and 71% of the tokens across ten runs. The spend concentrates in the verify-fix loop rather than in first implementation: the three priciest runs are all fix loops, four of eleven verified tasks failed their first panel, and the cheapest comparable run in the ledger is a verify_only re-panel at $0.36 against $1.22 for the same task's full round. The work is to make second and later rounds structurally cheaper: re-panel only the lenses that raised an upheld finding instead of the whole panel, pass the fixer a diff scoped to the finding's location rather than the full task context, and give each round a token ceiling read from the WorkItem budget so a loop that is not converging stops on cost and not only on round count. Land it with happy-path behavior unchanged — the exit test is that a task passing round 1 costs what it costs today while a task needing two fix rounds costs materially less, with the escalation contract untouched. This moves none of the three stated success metrics; it is a budget and kill-criteria matter and the Roadmap Gate should weigh it as such.

draft_work_items.title: Publish a calibration number for the risk router and the verifier lenses that fails when they rubber-stamp
draft_work_items.intent: Every spec this line has written routed low, the Spec Gate has never fired on a real run, and the panel's pass rate is reported as a feeling rather than a measurement. The raw material is already on disk: each run result records which lens raised which finding, whether it was upheld or overruled, and how many tasks failed their first round — 11 verified, 4 failed first round, 9 upheld, 2 overruled — but nothing aggregates it and ledger summary has no lens or router view. Two additions. First, a calibration report produced by /memory-roll: per lens, findings raised, upheld, overruled, and the share of tasks where that lens was the only one to raise anything; per router, the distribution of risk levels against the outcome those specs actually had, so a router that says low to everything shows up as a router whose low bucket contains the escalations. Second, a deliberate canary: inject a known defect into a task the panel has already passed and record whether the panel catches it, giving a catch rate that falls when a lens starts rubber-stamping — memory-roll's canary-inject node already exists to hang this on. The output must be a number in the ledger with a threshold, not a paragraph. This moves none of the three stated success metrics; it is how the line learns whether its own verdicts mean anything, and the Roadmap Gate should judge it on that.

draft_work_items.title: Declare each environment's required configuration and assert it before an env is called running
draft_work_items.intent: DELETE /items/:id answered 401 to 24 of 41 callers because ADMIN_TOKEN was never set on the environment, and the telemetry annotates this as 'not a defect' — which is the problem: a documented route was unusable for a whole window and every layer of the line read the environment as healthy. GET /health answers 200 regardless of configuration, so deploy start's readiness wait passes; the watch counts only 5xx and unreachable, so a uniformly 401 route scores clean; and the launch preflight's seven checks never look at the target environment's configuration at all. Give the Workspace an explicit required-configuration list per environment, seeded by /create-project from the app's documented routes (here: ADMIN_TOKEN for the admin DELETE), have substrate/deploy.js refuse to report an env as running when a declared variable is absent or empty, and add one preflight check in /launch that reads the list against the target env so a config-incomplete promotion is a NO-GO rather than a silent wall of 401s. Keep the app's own behavior unchanged — treating an unset token as 'no admin configured' is correct and should stay. This moves none of the three stated success metrics directly; it closes the gap between 'the process is running' and 'the service works', and it is the cheapest of the three deploy-visibility items in this batch.
